h1:
Phu Phan National Park
Waterfalls, caves, viewpoints and a cool-season mountain drive
intro: If you're in Sakon Nakhon during the cool season and want crisp mountain air with a lungful of nature, Phu Phan is the closest answer to town. The Phu Phan range runs along the border between Sakon Nakhon and Kalasin, with waterfalls, World War II-era caves, viewpoints that look down over the city and Nong Han Lake, and Route 213 that climbs the hills past one pretty curve after another. The park headquarters sits only about 25 km from town, so it's an easy self-drive. We'll walk you through the main sights, when to go for the best waterfalls, entry fees, the route, and where to camp if you want to spend a night up in the cool air.
chips: 🏞️ Views of the city + Nong Han Lake

blocks.html: Phu Phan National Park covers the forest along the Phu Phan range, spreading across several districts of Sakon Nakhon and reaching into Kalasin. It's a shady headwater forest, several degrees cooler than the town. The best part is how easy it is to get around: many of the sights sit right along Route 213 (Sakon Nakhon–Kalasin), so you can park and walk straight in without any hard trekking. It works both for people passing through on a half-day drive and for those who want to camp overnight in the cool air.

Phu Phan isn't a single spot — the sights are spread out along the ridge. Some are waterfalls, some are caves or rock plateaus, and some are roadside viewpoints. If you only have half a day, start with Kham Hom Waterfall and the snake-curve viewpoint, since they're close together and the easiest to reach.

items.name: Kham Hom Waterfall
items.blurb: The park's headline waterfall, fed from Khao Tham Dong Ling. It tumbles down pretty rock tiers in shady forest, the water is cool enough to play in, and there's a picnic area. About 18 km from town.

items.name: Snake-Curve Viewpoint
items.blurb: A hairpin bend on the mountain road near the Kham Hom Waterfall turnoff, looking down over Sakon Nakhon city and Nong Han Lake stretching to the horizon. It's the most popular photo stop on the drive.

items.name: Seri Thai Cave
items.blurb: A cave that served as a hideout and weapons store for the Free Thai (Seri Thai) movement during World War II. There are signboards telling the history, you can walk through, and the air inside is cool and quiet.

items.name: Lan Sao Eh
items.blurb: A broad rock plateau in the forest with oddly shaped boulders and a natural stone bridge nearby. It's good for a stroll and photos, and wildflowers come up across the plateau from late rainy season into early cool season.

items.name: Pha Sawoei
items.blurb: A roadside viewpoint on Route 213 on the Kalasin side, facing west. It's a popular rest stop for drivers crossing the Phu Phan hills, with food stalls and souvenir shops right there.

items.name: Preecha Suksan Waterfall
items.blurb: Another waterfall inside the park, smaller than Kham Hom and quieter. It suits anyone after a calmer corner, and the water is at its prettiest late in the rainy season.

blocks.title: Pick spots based on your time
blocks.html: Half a day → Kham Hom Waterfall + the snake curve is plenty · A full day → add Seri Thai Cave and Lan Sao Eh · Driving on to Kalasin → stop at Pha Sawoei as a rest break.

blocks.html: We'll be honest about the waterfalls: it all comes down to the season. They're fullest and most beautiful from late rainy season into early cool season, roughly October to early December, when the water is still strong, the forest is lush and green, and the air is starting to cool. If you come in the dry season (March–May) the waterfalls drop to a trickle or some run dry, and the appeal shifts to the viewpoints and caves instead.

If you're coming mainly for the cool weather, the best window is December to January. Mornings up on the mountain are properly cold, and on some days mist drifts along the forest. Drive up to a viewpoint early and you may catch a thin sea of mist over the city and Nong Han Lake. We'd suggest leaving town at first light if you want that shot.

items: Opening hours — the park is open roughly 08:00–18:00. Kham Hom Waterfall opens a little earlier, around 06:00–18:00. Aim to arrive before late afternoon so you have time to walk around at an easy pace.
Entry (Thai) — 20 THB adults, 10 THB children · 10 THB for pupils and students.
Vehicle fee — 30 THB for a four-wheel car · 20 THB for a motorbike · bicycles free.
Fee waived — children under 3, monks and clergy, seniors aged 60 and over, and people with disabilities.

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: These rates took effect around 2024 and may change under National Parks Department announcements. Some spots, such as Kham Hom Waterfall, may charge a fee separate from the park headquarters. If you're planning firm dates, call the park ahead on 086 459 5600 or 081 263 5029 to check.

The easiest way to see Phu Phan is to drive yourself, since the sights are spread along Route 213 (Sakon Nakhon–Kalasin). From Sakon Nakhon town, head out on Route 213 toward Kalasin. You'll pass Phu Phan Rajanivet Palace first, then the road starts climbing, and after about 25 km you reach the park headquarters. Along the way you'll come to turnoffs for Kham Hom Waterfall and the various viewpoints.

The climb is winding and steep in places. A sedan handles it fine at a sensible speed, but watch the hairpins like the snake curve. On cool-season mornings there can be mist that cuts visibility, so put your headlights on and drive a bit slower to be safe. If you don't have your own car, renting one or chartering a songthaew or motorbike taxi from town is the practical option, since there are few public buses that run directly to the sights.

blocks.title: Fuel up + stock up before you climb
blocks.html: There are few shops and petrol stations up on the mountain. Fill the tank and buy water and snacks for the car back in town, so you don't have to run back down to refuel partway.

blocks.text: Want to stay overnight up here?

blocks.html: If you really want to sleep in the cool Phu Phan air, the park has bungalows and a campground. Book ahead through the National Parks Department's online system (nps.dnp.go.th). The cool season gets busy, so reserve several weeks out. If you have your own tent you can pitch it for a per-person rate, or rent one from the park. Waking up on the mountain means cool air and thin mist you just won't get staying in town.

If you'd rather not camp, the other option is to stay in Sakon Nakhon town — which has hotels across a range of budgets — and drive up early in the morning. It's only about 25 km and takes under half an hour, which is handy if you want both a comfortable night and the morning views up on the mountain.

blocks.text: Good to know before you go

items: Wear hiking shoes — the paths to the waterfalls and rock plateaus get slippery when wet, so a grippy sole helps a lot.
Pack out your trash — this is a national park, so don't leave litter at the waterfalls or viewpoints.
Check the season first — come late rainy to early cool season for full waterfalls, December–January for the coldest air.
Patchy phone signal — coverage is weak in spots up on the mountain, so download offline maps beforehand for peace of mind.
Watch for wildlife and leeches in the rain — stick to the park's marked trails and don't wander off them.

faq.q: How far is Phu Phan National Park from Sakon Nakhon town, and is it a long drive?
faq.a: The park headquarters is on Route 213 (Sakon Nakhon–Kalasin), about 25 km from town — roughly a 30–40 minute drive, passing Phu Phan Rajanivet Palace before the road climbs the hills. Kham Hom Waterfall is closer, about 18 km from town.

faq.q: How much is entry to Phu Phan National Park?
faq.a: Thai visitors pay 20 THB for adults and 10 THB for children; foreign visitors pay 100 THB for adults and 50 THB for children, plus a vehicle fee of 30 THB for a four-wheel car or 20 THB for a motorbike. The fee is waived for monks, seniors aged 60 and over, people with disabilities, and children under 3. These rates took effect around 2024 and may change under National Parks Department announcements.

faq.q: When is the best time to see the Phu Phan waterfalls?
faq.a: Kham Hom Waterfall and the park's other falls are at their best and strongest from late rainy to early cool season, roughly October to early December. In the dry season (March–May) the water is low, but the viewpoints and caves are good to visit year-round. For the coolest air, come in December to January.

faq.q: Can you visit Phu Phan without your own car?
faq.a: Yes, but it takes a little planning, since few public buses run directly to the sights. The easiest options are to rent a car in Sakon Nakhon town, or charter a songthaew or motorbike taxi up. Driving yourself is the most flexible, as the sights are spread along Route 213.

faq.q: Can you stay overnight on Phu Phan?
faq.a: Yes — the park has bungalows and a campground, bookable through the National Parks Department's online system at nps.dnp.go.th. The cool season gets busy, so reserve several weeks ahead. Alternatively, stay at a hotel in Sakon Nakhon town and drive up early in the morning, since it's only about 25 km away.
